messages.subject: Fixed effect confidence interval with spde model
messages.subject_clean: Fixed effect confidence interval with spde model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,
I would like plotting the effect of a fixed effect and its confidence interval by ignoring the random term. I use a spatio-temporal spde model but I think the same goes for all model having random effect.

Below is a generic example for computing the confidence interval of the first fixed effect:
formulae <- (y~X1+X2+...+Xk+f(spatial,model=spde,group=spatial.group,control.group=list(model="ar1")))
mdl.spde <- inla(formulae, family="nbinomial", E=off7,data = data, control.fixed = list(correlation.matrix=TRUE),control.inla=list(lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix=TRUE))

newdata <- matrix(0,10,k)
newdata[,1] <- 1:10
colnames(newdata) <- c("X1","X2",...,"Xk")

formula.fixed <- (y~X1+X2+...+Xk)
mm<-model.matrix(formula.fixed[-2],as.data.frame(newdata))
V <- mdl.spde$misc$lincomb.derived.covariance.matrix
pred.se <http://pred.se> <- sqrt(diag(mm%*%tcrossprod(V,mm)))
pred.mean <- mm%*%mdl.spde$summary.fixed[,1]
plot(tab.var[,1],pred.mean)
lines(tab.var[,1],pred.mean+1.96*pred.se <http://pred.se>)
lines(tab.var[,1],pred.mean-1.96*pred.se <http://pred.se>)

This code gives wider confidence interval than expected from the standard errors displayed in the summary of the model.

Best wishes,
Kévin

We would like to implement a model where the dependent variable, which follows a Poisson distribution, depends on the following random effects and some other covariates:

y(i, j,t) = f{y(i,j,t-1),y(-i,j,t),y(-i,-j,t)} + other covariates

where i represents the space, j the sector of an economic activity and t the time. The idea is to analyse the variation of our dependent variable considering the temporal effect, the spatial effect, and the effect of an exogenous variable which depends both on the rest of the regions except i and on all the economic activities but j.

data1=list(field=mesh$idx$loc,year=period,Y=y1,y=y_ex)

formula = Y ~ f(field, model=spde,diagonal=diag.eps)+f(y, ???????)+f(year,model="rw1", diagonal=diag.eps)

Hi,

I think I can answer your questions. First point to note - the poly2nb() command does not automatically give everyone a neighbour - if there are single polygons islands in your shapefile it won't assign them neighbours, which is entirely appropriate as it would be inaccurate to assign them neighbours. Of course depending on your problem and the geography you may need to later assign everyone a neighbour but then again you may not.

You can visualize the nb matrix using:

plot(nb.map, coordinates(map))

Even with 3000 rows you should be able to spot islands and that may help you figure out which counties they are when comparing to a regular map - although that is very manual. But its generally good to visualise the nb matrix anyhow as I have found it can help spot other problems.

Alternatively to visualize polygon 19 for example you can do the following to fill it blue and leave the other polygon's blank:

plot(map)
plot(map[19,], add=TRUE, col="blue")

> >
> > > Q2, Are all FIPSs sorted before recoding in the graph file?
> >
> > I don't know how you have created the graph file...
>
> Here is the program:
>
> map <- readOGR("C:/lchien/Dropbox/diabetes/data/uscounty.shp","uscounty")
> nb.map <- poly2nb(map)
> nb2INLA("C:/lchien/Dropbox/asthma/data/uscounty.graph",nb.map)
>
> I checked the manuals of readOGR(), poly2nb(), and nb2INLA() functions, but found no related option to reorder my original FIPSs. In my imagination, if the original FIPS code is reordered first, and recoded to 1, 2, 3, ..., 3109 in the graph file, at least I can use this information to find out what is area #19's FIPS. If it is not reordered, I have no clue to find out the original FIPS of area #19.

The polygons are not sorted - so polygon 19 and relevant data should be accessible by subsetting the SPDF to row 19, e.g.:

map[19,]

I hope these answers are helpful,

James

>
>
>
>  > Q3. I referred some examples in this website, and see areas in some
> > > data sets are recoded with a variable starting from 0, not 1; however,
> > > the area code in its graph file starts from 1. I guess there might be
> > > some algorithms to match the inconsistent area codes between data and
> > > graph file, but I just feel confused on how to efficiently recode my
> > > original FIPSs? If I need to recode the original FIPS variable to
> > > match the area code in the graph file, again, like Q1, how can I know
> > > which FIPS is which area code?

> > this is historical. in the beginning of INLA the graph was coded as

> > a 1-based graph internally.

>
> inla1<-inla(distance~1+f(age,
> replicate=groupID),model="ar1"),data=mydata)
>
> Basically, I have time series data for multiple groups. I would like
> to fit an ar1 model but avoid assuming that the underlying ar1
> correlation is the same across all groups. I think using “replicate”
> assumes that it is, but I can't find much documentation about what
> “group” is doing?!

replicate produce iid replicates. group produce dependent replicates.
you can mix both, to produce iid replicates of dependent replicates.

the problem is that this is not well documented. I attach slides for
which this is all based upon. current group models are

> names(inla.models()$group)
[1] "exchangeable" "ar1"          "ar"           "rw1"
"rw2"
[6] "besag"

for an AR1 model, then if you group or replicate it, the the marginal
variance and the lag-one correlations are all the same. if they are all
different, you need to use multiple AR1 models.

Best
H

--
Håvard Rue

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Geographically weighted regression on R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Okango,

By using GWR in a set of 'n' areas, what it actually does is 'n'
regressions like:
    y = \beta_i  K(location_i - all_locations, window) x + e
and window is a parameter that you have to set select in some way.

In INLA you can have something called spatially varying coefficients (SVC)
   y = \beta_i x + e
where can have any spatial correlation structure. If you choose Besag,
you have
    \beta_i  ~  N(\sum_{j\sim i} \beta_j, 1/(n_i \tau))
i.e., the prior mean of \beta_i is the average over \beta_j, j:
neighbours of i

You can choose another spatial model instead.

To specify a Besag model for the regression coefficients for the
covariate 'STI', for example, you need to add in your formula a term like
   f(area_index, STI, model='besag')
So, the area index entry as first argument and the covariate values as
the second in f().

Elias.

No, the keyword here is "when doing prediction".  The second inla call

r = inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=1:10),family="poisson")

           control.mode=list(theta=r$mode$theta,restart=FALSE))

I'm using one of the forms in Gneiting 2002 at the moment, because
these have the advantage of being relatively simple, with a single
parameter beta controlling "space/time interaction" which can be 0
meaning none--very little is known in my application domain
(criminology) on the question we're trying to answer, so the first
step is descriptive statistics, model comparison between different
models, etc. Thus, I simply want to be able to compare a separable and
nonseparable model for my point process, keeping everything else the
same (so I don't want to adopt a mechanistic model).

I don't think I need spatial drift. Heat equations would be very neat,
but probably too fancy. What other types of nonseparability is/isn't
hard or in the works?

Thanks for the responses and very nice work on INLA by the way,
Seth
